        The auction schedule of RPM that has successfully driven efficient outcomes for

Exelon customers in the past has proven incapable of meeting the needs of the PJM Region

today and into the future. Customers in all six Exelon service territories are directly impacted

by the extraordinary prices produced by RPM in recent years, beginning with the 2025/2026

Delivery Year BRA that cleared at several multiples of the historical average capacity price in

PJM, and at roughly ten times the prior year’s clearing price. 12 The crisis has only deepened

since then, with the 2027/2028 and 2028/2029 Delivery Year BRAs clearing at the temporary

Commission-approved price cap and simultaneously falling thousands of MWs short of PJM’s

target Installed Reserve Margin. 13 While PJM’s staff, management, and Board of Managers

(“Board”) have diligently and competently administered RPM Auctions over the last two

decades, it is self-evident that RPM in its current structure is fundamentally broken. Not only

are PJM customers at large being forced to pay unprecedented prices for capacity, they are not

getting sufficient capacity in return, and are paying for a widening gap between supply and

demand as a reliability deficit looms.

        As the Commission correctly observed on September 30, 2026, “[w]e think it clear that

PJM’s ordinary instrument for procuring sufficient capacity to meet PJM’s reliability

requirement, the RPM, has failed to keep pace with the unprecedented influx of large load into

delivery completion, thereby structuralizing uncertainty and inaccuracy with no proportional

development schedules of today’s large loads, as well as the changing nature of market

dynamics and federal, state, and local environmental, permitting, and tax policies.

           The market outcomes produced under this paradigm create an unjustifiable chasm

between the costs customers pay and the capacity they receive, while simultaneously failing to

accurately portray the underlying supply and demand dynamics of the PJM Region in a manner

that inhibits efficient resource exit, and fails to incentivize efficient resource entry.

Accordingly, Exelon respectfully requests the Commission exercise its authority under FPA

section 206 to find the existing three-year forward period of RPM unjust and unreasonable,

and direct PJM to establish a just and reasonable “prompt” auction schedule, to run two months

before a given Delivery Year, starting with the 2030/2031 Delivery Year and continuing

a prompt auction schedule now, while this broader market redesign takes place, will have

several immediate benefits for the PJM Region:

       Exelon presents its legal case under FPA section 206 in Part IV of this complaint, which

is divided into two subparts. In Part IV.A, Exelon demonstrates that the three-year forward

period of RPM has become unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory or preferential under

FPA section 206, for the following five reasons:

       1. The risk balancing analysis the Commission relied on in 2006 to accept the load
          forecast inaccuracies inherent in RPM’s multi-year forward period has
          fundamentally collapsed in 2026.

       2. The prospective assumptions in 2006 regarding the ability of RPM’s multi-year
          forward period to incentivize Load-Serving Entity (“LSE”) bilateral contracting
          and risk hedging have been disproven over the course of 20 years.

       3. The current three-year forward period inhibits efficient resource exit and
          Deactivation, as it requires generator owners to invest in the absence of reasonable
          predictability in future operational capability and environmental policy.

       4. PJM’s current capacity accreditation methodology, Effective Load Carrying
          Capability (“ELCC”) bears no resemblance to the Equivalent Forced Outage Rate
          - demand (“eFORd”) model considered by the Commission in 2006, and the three-
          year forward period forces PJM to integrate speculative assumptions into its ELCC
          modeling.

       5. The current three-year forward period undermines the accuracy of other BRA
          planning parameters, including the assumed resource mix in each Locational
          Deliverability Area (“LDA”) used to calculate Capacity Emergency Transfer
          Objective (“CETO”) and Capacity Emergency Transfer Limit (“CETL”) values,
          leading to unjust and unreasonable results.

       In Part IV.B, Exelon requests that the Commission replace the three-year forward

period of RPM with a prompt auction, starting with the 2030/2031 Delivery Year and

continuing beyond. Exelon explains that a prompt auction is just and reasonable for the

following four reasons:

          accuracy of the price signal used in generator Deactivation decisions.

       3. A prompt auction will significantly enhance the quality of data used in PJM’s

       4. A prompt auction will significantly reduce the risks to new resources seeking to

 III.         BACKGROUND

             The concept of a multi-year forward period for RPM first emerged in PJM’s August

2005 Initial RPM Proposal, 24 and was designed to address one of several core deficiencies with

PJM’s then-existing capacity construct—namely that, as PJM explained, the construct did “not

look far enough into the future to secure capacity in time to meet reliability needs.” 25 In 2005,

this defect was glaring. At the time, PJM’s capacity construct only required that Capacity

Resources be committed for one day, and there was little incentive to commit for longer

periods. Moreover, Capacity Resources were permitted to “opt out” of their Capacity Resource

                iv.         PJM’s current capacity accreditation methodology (ELCC) bears no

           At the time of the Commission’s 2006 approval of RPM’s multi-year forward period,

PJM used a capacity accreditation methodology known as Equivalent Forced Outage Rate -

demand, or “eFORd.” This methodology focused on historic, unit-specific metrics that

measured the percentage of time that a specific unit was forced out of service or unable to run

when called upon. For various reasons, including the nature of the then-prevailing generation

mix and the types of operational risks faced by the PJM Region, eFORd was supportable when

RPM was accepted. Additionally, because eFORd relied on a resource’s own historical

performance rather than on system-wide, forward-looking modeling of the resource mix, it had

a high level of predictability, stability, and replicability for resource owners.

           On July 30, 2021, the Commission accepted PJM’s proposal to transition from eFORd

to a new capacity accreditation methodology, known as Effective Load Carrying Capability

(“ELCC”). 95 Unlike eFORd, ELCC considers the simultaneous reliability contribution of all

resources, and recognizes the complementary and antagonistic interactions among the

resource that contributes a significant level of capacity during high-risk hours (i.e., hours with

very high electricity demand and low resource output) will have a higher capacity value under

ELCC than a resource that delivers the same generating capability but only during low-risk

hours. These risk hours may vary as the resource mix changes (e.g., more wind and solar

resources are installed) and hours of high demand evolve (e.g., wide-scale electric car charging

at night). 96

model involves an extraordinary amount of data and analysis. 97 Specifically, ELCC class

accreditations are derived from sophisticated probabilistic modeling that estimates each

resource class’s reliability contribution across a wide range of system conditions, placing the

greatest weight on the hours of greatest reliability risk, and PJM must update and re-run this

analysis as the assumed resource mix and load profile change from year to year. 98

decline significantly across upcoming Delivery Years as PJM’s assumptions about extended

also experiencing meaningful changes. This dynamic can be seen in Figure 4 of the Nicholson

along with PJM’s preliminary estimate for Delivery Years 2030/2031 and 2031/2032.

 assumptions used, such as the assumed resource mix and system loads. Because even modest

shifts in ELCC accreditation can translate into substantial swings in a resource’s qualifying

capacity, and, in the aggregate, in the auction’s supply curve and clearing price, basing those

accreditation values on three-and-a-half-year-old assumptions introduces significant

inaccuracy into the BRA that a shorter forward period would not. 103 Owing to the resulting

inaccuracies, BRA prices can diverge from what underlying supply and demand fundamentals

would otherwise produce, rendering the current three-year forward period unjust and

unreasonable.

                   v.         The current three-year forward period undermines the accuracy of
                              other BRA planning parameters, including the assumed resource mix in
                              each Locational Deliverability Area used to calculate CETO/CETL
                              values, leading to unjust and unreasonable results.

            The planning parameters used in a given BRA play a critical role in the auction’s

outcome. For example, RPM utilizes an administratively set demand curve—the Variable

Resource Requirement Curve (“VRR Curve”)—which represents the prices that consumers

should be willing to pay for varying quantities of capacity. In developing the demand curve

for a given BRA, PJM forecasts the expected peak load for a particular Delivery Year and then

sets a target level of capacity needed to reliably serve the load—also known as the Reliability

Requirement—given the expected resource portfolio. The auction’s supply curve is based on

Sell Offers for capacity that Capacity Market Sellers submit at a specific price and, together,

the offers comprise the auction’s supply curve. RPM is a locational market, meaning there are

defined areas within the PJM Region that have limits on the amount of capacity they can

import. Those areas are LDAs, which recognize and quantify the locational value of capacity




103
      Id., at ¶¶ 46, 49-50.



                                                    44
 within the PJM Region. As relevant here, the modeled LDAs are determined by comparing

the import limit of an LDA (CETL) with the amount of capacity that needs to be imported into

a LDA to meet the reliability criterion (CETO). Sell Offers are located in specific LDAs based

on where those resources are located.

            The accuracy of the planning parameters used in a given auction are only as good as

the data upon which they are based. As Dr. Nicholson explains, the three-year forward period

undermines the accuracy of certain planning parameters, including CETO and CETL, because

these values depend on assumptions about the resource mix and transmission topology that

will actually exist in each LDA during the Delivery Year. 104 As with the ELCC and load

forecast inputs discussed above, these assumptions are far less reliable when projected three

and a half years in advance than when set closer to the Delivery Year. These inaccuracies and

uncertainties introduced into the CETO and CETL parameters can, in turn, lead to capacity

prices that do not reflect market fundamentals in the Delivery Year by misrepresenting the

transmission system’s ability to transfer capacity. 105 This can lead to unjust and unreasonable

outcomes. Indeed, the idea that inaccurate planning parameters can warp the outcome of a

given BRA and disassociate it from basic market fundamentals is unfortunately not an

academic one. In December 2022, PJM discovered that certain Planned Generation Capacity

Resources and planned Intermittent Resources in the DPL South LDA did not offer into the

2024/2025 Delivery Year BRA, notwithstanding the fact that such resources were included by

PJM years earlier in the modeling assumptions (CETO) that formed the DPL South LDA

Reliability Requirement. The absence of these resources from the 2024/2025 BRA resulted in



104
      Id., at ¶ 52.
105
      Id.



                                                45
 an overstated LDA Reliability Requirement, and led to a dramatically higher clearing price

that was wholly unrepresentative of the actual capacity needs of the LDA. 106                   As the

Independent Market Monitor (“IMM”) described it, the clearing prices for DPL South “do not

reflect the actual market supply and demand fundamentals, overstate the local reliability

requirement, serve no useful purpose, and are therefore unjust and unreasonable.” 107

           Accordingly, the three-year forward period of RPM is unjust and unreasonable, because

it undermines the accuracy of important BRA planning parameters, including the assumed

resource mix in each LDA used to calculate CETO/CETL values, leading to market outcomes

divorced from underlying supply and demand conditions.

           B.      The Commission Should Adopt a Prompt Auction Schedule as the Just and
                   Reasonable Replacement Rate.

           In the event that the Commission finds the three-year forward period of RPM to be

unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory or preferential under FPA section 206, Exelon

proposes the Commission direct PJM to adopt as a replacement rate a “prompt” BRA schedule,

to run two months before a given Delivery Year, starting with the 2030/2031 Delivery Year

BRA, currently scheduled for May 2027, and beyond. The Commission need not treat this

proposal as novel or untested. To the contrary, the Commission has already found, on at least

three occasions—for all of the other centralized capacity market structures in its jurisdiction—

that a prompt capacity auction schedule is just and reasonable. Most recently, on March 30,

2026, the Commission accepted ISO-NE’s proposal, filed jointly with the New England Power

Participants Committee, to replace its three-year forward capacity market with a prompt



106
      See generally Docket No. ER23-729-000.
107
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Comments of the Independent Market Monitor of PJM, Docket No. ER23-729-
000 (Jan. 20, 2023).



                                                  46
 capacity market in which an Annual Capacity Auction is held approximately one month before

the relevant Capacity Commitment Period, effective March 31, 2026. 108 In accepting ISO-

NE’s proposal, the Commission expressly relied on its prior orders finding that MISO’s prompt

capacity auction schedule, under which MISO holds its auction two months before the delivery

year, is just and reasonable. 109 The Commission has likewise accepted prompt auctions relying

on near-term procurement in NYISO. 110 For the reasons discussed below, moving to a prompt

schedule in PJM will provide the same substantial benefits, and particularly so in the dynamic

and uncertain environment currently facing the PJM Region.

                   i.        A prompt auction will significantly improve the accuracy of key BRA
                             auction parameters, resulting in capacity prices that better reflect
                             actual supply and demand fundamentals and system conditions in the
                             Delivery Year.

           A prompt auction schedule will significantly enhance the accuracy of key BRA auction

parameters, thereby resulting in capacity prices that better reflect actual market fundamentals

and system conditions in the Delivery Year. As Dr. Nicholson explains, a shorter forward

period would reduce forecast uncertainty across each of the BRA’s key inputs. Specifically, it

would allow PJM to forecast peak demand closer to the Delivery Year, reducing the risk of

over-forecasting load and procuring more capacity than is actually needed, while also allowing

PJM to base ELCC accreditation values on a resource mix and system conditions that are far

more likely to reflect what will actually exist during the Delivery Year rather than a three-and-




108
      See ISO-NE Order, at P 1.
109
    Id., at P 32 (MISO Order, at PP 70-74 (finding that MISO’s prompt capacity auction market design may be
beneficial because “[load-serving entities] can accurately forecast their loads by taking into consideration changes
such as those resulting from shifting economic conditions and MISO can accurately account for transmission
constraints, forced outage rates, and expected performance of Load Modifying Resources”); MISO Rehearing
Order, at PP 125-26).
110
      See N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 179 FERC ¶ 61,102, at PP 2-3 (2022).



                                                        47
 a-half-year-old projection. 111 It would also improve the accuracy of CETO/CETL values and

the resulting Local Deliverability Area Reliability Requirements, which likewise depend on

assumptions about the future resource mix and transmission topology. 112

            The net effect of this enhanced accuracy in BRA auction parameters is self-evident—

capacity prices that better reflect actual market fundamentals and system conditions. The

Commission has previously found this policy outcome to be just and reasonable. Specifically,

in accepting ISO-NE’s prompt auction schedule, the Commission found that the shorter

forward period would “reduce demand uncertainty because the Installed Capacity Requirement

will be calculated using data that is closer in time to the Capacity Commitment Period” and

would “result in more accurate Qualified Capacity values for resource accreditation.” 113

Similarly, in the Commission’s order accepting MISO’s prompt auction schedule as just and

reasonable, the Commission found that “MISO’s prompt Auction design allows load

forecasting to occur within the year leading up to the Planning Year.” 114 The Commission

acknowledged the inherent benefits of this change, finding that “LSEs can accurately forecast

their loads by taking into consideration changes such as those resulting from shifting economic

conditions and MISO can accurately account for transmission constraints, forced outage rates,

and expected performance of Load Modifying Resources.” 115

            The same legal and policy rationale the Commission used in the ISO-NE Order and the

MISO Order apply with equal if not greater force here. The closer in time that PJM establishes

its Installed Reserve Margin, ELCC accreditation values, CETO/CETL, and other key BRA

auction parameters to the actual Delivery Year, the more those parameters will reflect the

resource mix, load conditions, and system topology that actually exist, rather than a years-old

projection of what they might be. These rationales are only strengthened by the rapidly

changing conditions currently facing the PJM Region; that is, the demands of large loads and

associated forecasting challenges, as well as the evolving resource mix and a shifting policy

environment.

                  ii.         A prompt auction will significantly enhance the quality of information
                              and the accuracy of the price signal used in generator Deactivation
                              decisions.

           By definition, a prompt auction schedule narrows the window across which resource

owners must attempt to forecast future operational, environmental, regulatory, and market

conditions when deciding whether and how to bid into a BRA and commit their Capacity

Resources for a Delivery Year. As explained by Dr. Nicholson, this in turn enhances the

quality and accuracy of the price signal that RPM sends to those resource owners in two distinct

ways. 116

           First, it increases the economic efficiency of resource exit from the market. This

enhanced efficiency in market exit will become increasingly important in the PJM Region in

the coming years, as a substantial volume of existing capacity in the PJM Region is expected

to reach the end of its useful life and retire. 117 Some aging capacity has been kept operational



116
      See Nicholson Affidavit, at ¶ 57.
117
      Id.; See also PJM White Paper, at 16.



                                                    49
 in response to high prices. Additional capacity has been kept operational by out-of-market

mechanisms, such as RMR arrangements and FPA section 202c orders from the Department

of Energy, but these interventions are, by definition, temporary and not designed as primary

tools to achieve long-term resource adequacy. Furthermore, as generating assets continue to

age, keeping them operational will become prohibitively expensive, their operations will

become even more challenging, and the resulting policy goal should be to manage their exit,

not keep them online indefinitely. To this point, the Commission has previously found

proposals that increase the efficiency of economic market entry and exit to be just and

reasonable. 118

            Second, a prompt auction allows resource owners that choose to remain in the market

to “de-risk” their capacity supply offers by removing the need to price in the multi-year

“operational and policy-uncertainty” premium described above in Section IV.A.iii. 119 This

should apply downward pressure to capacity prices.

            In short, the shift to a prompt structure will significantly enhance the quality of

information and the accuracy of the investment signal used in resource owner market exit and

Deactivation decisions. Specifically, a prompt structure will allow commitment decisions to

be based on more current information, which will allow resource owners to better assess a

Capacity Resource’s remaining economic life, operating condition, needed capital


118
    See e.g. Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., 187 FERC ¶ 61,102, at P 80 (2024) (finding MISO’s
RBDC proposal to adopt a sloped demand curve in the Auction to be just in reasonable in part because it will

other reasons), modified on denial of reh’g by Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., 189 FERC P
61159 (2024); ISO New England, Inc., 173 FERC ¶ 61,161, at PP 48–50 (2020) (agreeing on rehearing that a
capacity market design “appropriately allows the [Forward Capacity Market] to provide the proper price signal
to trigger entry and exit of capacity supply resources,” and finding that the Commission had properly “considered
... whether the [Forward Capacity Market] provides the proper price signals to trigger appropriate entry and exit
of capacity resources”).
119

 improvements, and market risks (e.g., Capacity Performance risk), producing in aggregate

outcomes that better reflect the actual state of the PJM fleet as it ages, and capacity prices that

more accurately reflect the avoidable going forward costs of resources.

                      iii.    A prompt auction schedule will significantly enhance the quality of data
                              used in PJM’s ELCC capacity accreditation, thereby better aligning
                              both price and payments with resource contributions to resource
                              adequacy.

            Another important benefit to a prompt auction schedule is the enhanced quality of the

data inputs used in PJM’s ELCC capacity accreditation process. PJM’s capacity accreditation

methodology has grown substantially more complex and data-intensive since the Commission

first approved the current multi-year forward period in 2006. As noted above, in 2021 the

Commission approved PJM’s transition from its longstanding eFORd methodology to an

ELCC approach.               In 2024 the Commission accepted PJM’s proposal to make further

enhancements by transitioning to a “marginal” ELCC framework and extending ELCC

accreditation to all Generation Capacity Resources.                     In doing so, the Commission

acknowledged a key underlying concern with ELCC in relation to the RPM’s three-year

forward period—namely that “PJM’s RPM aims to ensure resource adequacy for a future

delivery year, and as such, there will inevitably be differences between the resource mix

forecasted at the time of the auction and the actual, cleared resource mix.” 120 Nonetheless, the

Commission found that PJM had demonstrated that any differences between the forecasted and

cleared resource mix are unlikely to introduce significant capacity accreditation errors. 121

Specifically, the Commission found that, based on PJM’s sensitivity analysis at the time, the

forecast error was likely to be a “negligible amount” (an estimated 115 MW out of a 170,000

121
      Id., at P 76.



                                                       51
 MW system). 122 As discussed above in Section IV.A.iv, data over the last two years has

disproven this assumption. 123

            Adopting a prompt auction will significantly improve the quality of data used in PJM’s

ELCC modeling, thereby better addressing the Commission’s original concern in 2024

regarding the “differences between the resource mix forecasted at the time of the auction and

the actual, cleared resource mix.” 124 As Dr. Nicholson explains, because a prompt auction

would base ELCC accreditation on a resource mix and system conditions far closer to the actual

Delivery Year, this will lead to superior economic outcomes by reducing both over- and under-

accreditation of resources and the resulting mispricing of capacity. 125 Indeed, the Commission

has already found that a prompt auction schedule produces more accurate capacity

accreditation values, including in the ISO-NE Order where the Commission found as just and

reasonable a prompt auction schedule that would “result in more accurate Qualified Capacity

values for resource accreditation.” 126

            Finally, a prompt auction schedule will allow Capacity Resources that have previously

received a capacity commitment to have their accreditation values recalculated annually, using

more up-to-date data. This provides several benefits, including ensuring that a resource’s

accredited capacity value reflects the resource mix and system conditions that actually prevail

closer to the Delivery Year, rather than a three-and-a-half-year-old projection, giving resource

      Nicholson Affidavit, at ¶ 58.

      ISO-NE Order, at P 32.

 owners better information with which to construct their capacity supply offers and plan

maintenance and retirement decisions, and reducing the risk that a resource is over- or under-

credited relative to its true reliability contribution.

                      iv.     A prompt auction will significantly reduce the risks to new resources
                              seeking to enter the market by creating more certainty regarding their
                              expected availability for the Delivery Year.

            A prompt auction will significantly reduce the risks, for customers and suppliers,

associated with the timing of new resources entering the market, as resources will have more

certainty about their expected availability for each Delivery Year, and particularly their first

Delivery Year in service. This will directly address the problem that the Commission has

previously described as “phantom entry,” where resources that receive a capacity commitment

years in advance are not actually operational in time for the delivery period. 127 As the Filing

Parties explained in the ISO-NE proceeding, this phantom entry problem can raise capacity

prices when the risk of non-commercial operation is priced into capacity offers. 128

            As explained by Dr. Nicholson, to the extent that it exists in PJM, a prompt auction

would directly address the problem of “phantom entry” by allowing only those resources that

have actually achieved, or are on the imminent path to achieving, commercial operation to

participate, rather than requiring new entrants to make a binding capacity commitment years

before they can demonstrate they will actually be available. 129 This will provide both PJM and

Market Participants with far greater certainty regarding actual resource availability for the

applicable Delivery Year.




127

128
      Id., at P 13.
129
      Nicholson Affidavit, at ¶ 59.

 V.         REFUND EFFECTIVE DATE

           As discussed above, Exelon respectfully requests that the Commission establish a

refund effective date of January 1, 2027, and permit Fast Track processing under Rule 206(h)

to facilitate a Commission order by no later than January 31, 2027—currently the last day

before the posting of the planning parameters for the 2030/31 Delivery Year BRA.

VI.        RULE 206 REQUIREMENTS

           To the extent not already provided above, Exelon provides the following additional

information required by Rule 206 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure. 130

Exelon respectfully requests waiver of any part of the Commission’s regulations necessary to

process this filing.

           A.       Good faith estimate of financial impact or harm (Rule 206(b)(4))

           The complaint sets forth in detail above the financial impact and harm to PJM Market

Participants caused by the three-year forward period of RPM.

           B.       Practical, operational, or nonfinancial impacts (Rule 206(b)(5))

           The practical, operational, and nonfinancial impacts of the RPM’s three-year forward

period are described at length in the sections above.

           C.       Whether the matters are pending in any other FERC proceeding or other
                    forum (Rule 206(b)(6))

           The issue of whether the three-year forward period of RPM has become unjust and

unreasonable under FPA section 206, as presented in this complaint, is not to Exelon’s

knowledge pending in any other existing Commission proceeding or forum in which Exelon is

a party.




130
      18 C.F.R. § 385.206.



                                                 54
          D.      Specific relief or remedy requested (Rule 206(b)(7))

         The complaint sets forth in detail the specific relief requested.

         E.      Documents supporting the complaint (Rule 206(b)(8))

         This filing consists of the following:

         •    This Transmittal Letter;

         •    Affidavit of Dr. Emma Nicholson, included as Attachment A;

         •    Affidavit of Deborah M. Sears, included as Attachment B; and

         •    A Form of Notice, included as Attachment C.

         F.      Use of alternative dispute resolution (Rule 206(b)(9))

         Exelon has not used the Enforcement Hotline, Dispute Resolution Service, tariff-based

dispute resolution mechanisms, or other informal dispute resolution procedures, because the

complaint argues that the three-year forward period of RPM is no longer just and reasonable,

and is therefore unlawful under FPA section 206. Only the Commission has the legal authority

to provide the statutory remedy that the complaint requests. For this reason, Exelon does not

believe that alternative dispute resolution (“ADR”) under the Commission’s supervision could

successfully resolve the complaint, nor could any specific ADR procedures. Exelon has not

agreed to any process for resolving the complaint outside of the instant proceeding.

         G.      Notice (Rule 206(b)(10))

         Exelon has appended a form of notice of this filing for publication in the Federal

Register, in accordance with the specifications in section 385.203(d) of the Commission’s

rules.

         H.      Request for Fast Track Processing (Rule 206(b)(11))

         As described above, Exelon respectfully requests that the Commission permit Fast

Track processing under Rule 206(h) to facilitate a Commission order by no later than January



                                                  55
 31, 2027—currently the last day before the posting of the planning parameters for the 2030/31

Delivery Year BRA.

VII.   SERVICE AND NOTICE

       In accordance with Rule 206(c), Exelon has served a copy of this complaint upon PJM,

as Respondent, simultaneously with the filing of the complaint.

VIII. CONCLUSION

       Wherefore, for the foregoing reasons, Exelon respectfully requests that the

Commission: (i) find under FPA section 206 that the current three-year forward period of

PJM’s RPM is no longer just and reasonable; (ii) adopt as a replacement rate a “prompt”

auction schedule, to run two months before a given Delivery Year, starting with the 2030/2031

Delivery Year and continuing beyond; (iii) establish a refund effective date of January 1, 2027;

and (iv) permit Fast Track processing under Rule 206(h) to facilitate a Commission order by

no later than January 31, 2027—currently the last day before the posting of the planning

parameters for the 2030/31 Delivery Year BRA.

                            AFFIDAVIT OF DR. EMMA NICHOLSON
                           ON BEHALF OF EXELON CORPORATION

1. My name is Dr. Emma Nicholson, Ph.D., and my business address is 1201 F St, NW,
   Washington, DC 20004. I am a Principal in the Energy Practice of Charles River Associates
   (“CRA”). In this affidavit, I provide evidence and analysis in support of Exelon Corporation’s
   (“Exelon”) complaint in this proceeding.

   I.      QUALIFICATIONS

2. I joined CRA in July 2025 and have been continuously employed ever since. At CRA, I
   support electric utilities, data center developers, and state commissions in matters related to
   wholesale electricity markets, with a focus on PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”). I have
   also supported grid operators with wholesale electricity market design issues and other matters
   related to transmission planning.

3. Prior to this position, I served as Senior Economic Advisor to the Office of Energy Policy and
   Innovation at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), where
   I worked with staff to advise the Commission on wholesale electricity and ancillary services
   market design, capacity market design, Capacity Resource accreditation, and other matters. At
   the Commission, I also served as an Economist and in other roles. I also have prior consulting
   experience in the energy practices of economic consulting firms.

4. I hold a BA in economics and government and politics from the University of Maryland at
   College Park, and an MA and Ph.D in economics from Georgetown University. My CV is
   attached as Exhibit EN-4.
    II.      TESTIMONY
5. My testimony is divided into four parts, Parts A, B, C, and D. In Part A, I provide a general
   assessment of the current state of the PJM capacity market, the Reliability Pricing Model
   (“RPM”). 1 In Part B, I provide evidentiary support and analysis for each of the five arguments
   identified in the complaint as to why the current three-year forward period of RPM is no longer
   just and reasonable. In Part C, I provide evidentiary support and analysis for each of the four
   arguments identified in the complaint as to why a “prompt” auction schedule is just and
   reasonable. Finally, in Part D, I provide analysis on general market design considerations
   regarding the implementation of a prompt capacity auction in PJM.

         A. General Assessment of the Current State of RPM.

6. PJM’s capacity construct is experiencing profound challenges. The last two primary capacity
   auctions, or Base Residual Auctions (“BRAs”), cleared considerably short of the Reliability
   Requirement. PJM is now undertaking efforts to address the problem in the short term through
   the Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) proposal, which the Commission has accepted
   and suspended for further briefing. In this Part A, I summarize current conditions in PJM’s
   capacity market.

7. BRA prices have increased significantly in recent years, as shown in Figure 1 below. The
   “Rest of RTO” PJM capacity price, a benchmark capacity price that most PJM zones pay,
   increased significantly starting with the 2025/26 BRA. 2 This price increase ultimately resulted
   in complaints and PJM proposing a price collar that the Commission accepted to be in place
   for the 2026/27 through 2029/30 BRAs. Since the collar was imposed, all successive BRAs
   have cleared at the price cap. For example, the most recent BRA was the 2028/29 BRA, held
   in July 2026, and it cleared at the price cap of $325.00/MW-day. 3 The 2028/29 BRA did not
   procure enough capacity to meet the region’s Reliability Requirement, clearing 6,831 MW of
   unforced capacity (“MW UCAP”) short of the Reliability Requirement. This was the second
   BRA that failed to procure the Reliability Requirement, with the 2027/28 BRA also having
   cleared 6,517 MW UCAP short of the Reliability Requirement. 4 Absent the price collar, the
   2027/28 BRA would have cleared at $529.80/MW-day in all zones. In the 2028/29 BRA, the
   Rest of RTO price would have been $554.72/MW-day, the Dominion zone would have cleared

        B. Evidence and Analysis Supporting the Conclusion that the Current Three-Year
           Forward Period of RPM is No Longer Just and Reasonable.

11. Circumstances have changed significantly since 2006, when the Commission found the BRA’s
    current three-year forward period to be just and reasonable. As explained further below, these
    changes have accumulated over the last twenty years and include increased load growth
    uncertainty, longer generator development timelines, and changes in RPM market rules. As
    such, the balancing and expectations the Commission relied upon when it found the BRA’s
    three-year forward period to be just and reasonable no longer hold.

12. As I explain below, holding the BRA three years before the delivery period unnecessarily
    exposes PJM Market Participants to increased risks and uncertainties on both the demand side
    and the supply side. These risks result solely from a market design choice and could be
    avoided, or at the very least significantly reduced, with a shorter forward period. Holding the
    BRA three years prior to the Delivery Year (38 months to be exact) requires estimating BRA
    parameters over three years in advance, results in less accurate load forecasts and capacity
    resource accreditation, and impacts other key auction parameters, further divorcing the auction
    parameters and resulting clearing prices from supply and demand fundamentals and system
    conditions.

          i.    The risk balancing analysis the Commission relied on in 2006 to accept the load
                forecast inaccuracies inherent in RPM’s multi-year forward period has
                fundamentally collapsed in 2026.

                     a. Load forecast uncertainty

14. The level of uncertainty in PJM’s near-term load forecast has increased dramatically since
    2006, when the Commission initially accepted the BRA’s three-year forward period. The data
    I present below demonstrate that current load growth projections, principally from large loads
    such as data centers, are likely to overstate the peak load forecast PJM uses to determine the
    Reliability Requirement, and thus the amount of capacity PJM procures in the BRA. Procuring
    too much capacity in the BRA unnecessarily increases costs for PJM Market Participants,
    because if a portion of the large loads included in the BRA load forecast does not materialize,
    capacity cost increases will be borne by all remaining customers. This outcome would be
    inefficient because the region would purchase more capacity than is necessary to achieve
    resource adequacy targets, and likely at higher prices than the fundamentals would support.
    The risks of over-forecasting data center loads are particularly acute today, as data center
    projects are encountering increasing delays driven by additional state requirements for data
    center development, siting and permitting challenges, greater local community opposition, and
    supply chain constraints. 13 Importantly, uncertainty associated with data center load growth is
    not unique to PJM; grid operators across the U.S. face similar challenges in forecasting large
    load growth stemming from similarly high degrees of uncertainty nationwide.

16. The historical load forecast changes between the BRA and the 3rd IA do not reflect a
    shortcoming of PJM or its prior load forecasting methods. No amount of modeling can
    eliminate the uncertainty inherent in forecasting peak loads in a 12-month Delivery Year over
    three years in advance, even without large load growth uncertainty. Rather, the increase in
    BRA load forecast precision shown in Figure 2 reflects the shorter forecast horizon; the
    2023/24 through 2026/27 BRAs had a shorter forward period and smaller adjustments between
    the BRA and the IA, which suggests that the load forecasts used for the 2023/24 through
    2026/27 BRAs were more accurate than prior BRAs with a three-year forward period.

44. At the time of the Commission’s 2006 approval of RPM’s multi-year forward period, PJM
    used a capacity accreditation methodology known as Equivalent Forced Outage Rate - demand,
    or “eFORd.” This methodology focused on historic, unit-specific metrics that measured the
    percentage of time that a specific unit was forced out of service or unable to run when called

    than on system-wide, forward-looking modeling of the resource mix, it had a fairly high level

    in January 2024. 67 Unlike eFORd, ELCC considers the simultaneous reliability contribution

    resources expected to be able to provide capacity in a given Delivery Year. In general, a

    probability of a capacity shortage) will have a higher capacity value under ELCC than a
    resource that delivers the same generating capability but only during low-risk hours. These
    risk hours may vary as the resource mix changes (e.g., more wind and solar resources are
    installed) and hours of high demand evolve (e.g., wide-scale electric car charging at night).

51. Beyond the load forecast and ELCC accreditation discussed above, other BRA planning
    parameters play a critical role in the market outcomes. For example, the BRA is a locational
    market and reflects the fact that the transfer of capacity between zones in a given BRA is
    limited by the amount of transfer capability between zones. PJM defines Locational
    Deliverability Areas (“LDAs”) where those transfer limits might bind, and constrain imports
    into that LDA, possibly causing the LDA to clear at a higher price than other PJM regions (i.e.,
    price separation). Prior to each BRA, PJM performs studies to determine each LDA’s
    Reliability Requirement by adding Capacity Emergency Transfer Objective (“CETO”) to the
    capacity within the LDA. PJM also calculates each LDA’s Capacity Emergency Transfer
    Limit (“CETL”), which is the amount of capacity the LDA can import from other regions
    during peak conditions. The CETO and CETL are important BRA parameters because if an
    LDA’s CETL is below its CETO, the LDA must meet a portion of its Reliability Requirement
    with resources within the LDA. Generally speaking, a lower CETL means that the LDA must
    meet a higher portion of its Reliability Requirement with internal resources, which can result
    in higher capacity prices than other PJM regions if the LDA must purchase capacity from
    internal resources that are more expensive than the capacity available in neighboring regions.

AFFIDAVIT OF DEBORAH M SEARS
ON BEHALF OF EXELON CORPORATION

My name is Deborah Sears, and my business address is 500 N Wakefield Drive, Newark, DE
19702. I currently serve as the Senior Manager, Energy Acquisition, in the Governmental,
Regulatory and External Affairs group of Pepco Holdings, LLC, which is an indirect wholly-
owned subsidiary of Exelon Corporation (“Exelon”) and which itself owns Atlantic City
Electric Company (“ACE”), Delmarva Power & Light Company (“DPL”), and Potomac
Electric Power Company (“Pepco” and collectively with ACE and DPL, the “Exelon PHI
Companies”). I am submitting this affidavit in support of Exelon’s complaint in this
proceeding.

1. Specifically, in this affidavit, I:

a. Provide a general overview of the Exelon PHI Companies’ procurement
responsibilities as Load Serving Entities (“LSEs”), focusing on several of Exelon’s
operating jurisdictions where I have experience; and

b. Describe the constraints and limitations imposed by state law and regulation on the
ability of Exelon LSEs to engage in long-term bilateral contracting and risk hedging
to mitigate the risk of high clearing prices in PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s
(“PJM”) Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”).

I. QUALIFICATIONS
2. I joined Exelon in 2023 and have been continuously employed ever since. As Senior

Manager, Energy Acquisition, I am responsible for overseeing the procurement and
settlement of supply for the Exelon PHI Companies, which include ACE, DPL, and Pepco.

 3.

I.

Prior to joining Exelon, my experience includes 13 years of wholesale energy experience,
working at Exelon PowerTeam, later as Constellation, in various roles, including
accounting, power scheduling, generation dispatch, energy trading, and commercial
transactions where I participated in long-term contract negotiation and administration, load
auctions, and other projects. During my time in these roles, I also held certifications as a
PJM Generation Operator and NERC Reliability Coordinator.

Thold a Bachelor of Science in Accounting from The Pennsylvania State University.
TESTIMONY OF DEBORAH M SEARS
A. Exelon LSEs’ Procurement Responsibilities

The Exelon PHI Companies are responsible for providing Standard Offer Service (“SOS”)
(Basic Generation Service (“BGS”) in New Jersey) within the ACE, DPL, and Pepco
service territories within Maryland, Delaware, New Jersey, and the District of Columbia
(“DC”) for customers who do not select a competitive supplier. In order to provide these
services, the Exelon PHI Companies must procure wholesale energy, capacity, ancillary
services, and sufficient Renewable Energy Credits (“RECs”) required to meet Renewable
Portfolio Standards (“RPS”) within each jurisdiction.

Supply is procured through auction processes. The procedure to procure supply differs for
each of these jurisdictions but all such processes are regulated by the applicable state utility
regulatory commissions.

Maryland and Delaware each require procurement of supply for residential and small
commercial customer classes for a two-year period, while the District of Columbia and
New Jersey procure for a three-year period. Large commercial contracts have a tenor of
one year in all jurisdictions except for Maryland, where they procure 3-month contracts.
Within these auctions, suppliers are bidding on a slice of load basis, and “slices” are
separated into tranches representing approximately 50 MW of capacity. The results of the
winning bids are then averaged to determine the SOS/BGS price for the upcoming energy
year. Maryland, the District of Columbia, and New Jersey all have a full requirements
product, while Delaware is energy, ancillary services, and capacity only. The auctions
themselves also differ in methodology, but all are structured to procure the lowest cost
supply for customers.

The auctions are all monitored by a market monitoring unit and results are approved by the
applicable state utility regulatory commission.

B. Constraints and Limitations Imposed by State Law and Regulation on the Ability
of Exelon’s LSEs to Engage in Long-Term Bilateral Contracting and Risk
Hedging.

The SOS/BGS auction structures are highly prescriptive and any changes to the annual
auction process are reviewed through a stakeholder meeting called the Procurement

 Improvement Process, and the final changes to the Request for Proposal and Full
Requirements Service Agreement require approval by the applicable state utility regulatory
commission. Pepco, DPL, and ACE are not permitted to enter into any bilateral
transactions, including hedging agreements, without approval from the applicable state
utility regulatory commission. Below, for each state, I describe the general contracting
constraints and, as appropriate, offer recent examples where the regulator has directed
specific contracting activities

10. In Maryland, utilities are not permitted to bilaterally contract unless first directed to do so
by statute or through a Maryland Public Service Commission (“Maryland PSC”) approved
procurement program, like the current SOS program. In April 2026, the Maryland PSC
began conducting a study through the Renewable Energy Certainty Act (“RECA”)! to
evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of different generation procurement models,
which include long-term contracting structures. It is unclear at this stage which, if any, of
these programs will ultimately be advanced by the Maryland PSC.

11. In Delaware, the SOS requirements are described in Order 6746.2 As in the case of
Maryland, DPL does not have the ability to bilaterally contract within Delaware unless it
is first approved by the Delaware Public Service Commission. However, without
legislative changes, any DPL expense related to a long-term contract would only be
allocated to SOS customers, making long-term contracting cost prohibitive because any
associated costs could only be recovered from SOS customers, not from those receiving
service from a third-party supplier or a cooperative.

12. New Jersey provides the guidelines for BGS within the Electric Discount and Energy
Competition Act, section 48:3-57, which also restricts bilateral contracting. As part of the
Clean Energy Act of 2018, New Jersey launched the Garden State Energy Storage Program
(“GSESP”), which is a multi-phase program designed to deploy 2,000 MW of energy
storage by 2030, but this is a specific, statutorily directed procurement.

13. Finally, the District of Columbia also restricts bilateral contracting outside of SOS, as
described in the Code of the District of Columbia Section 34-1509, Standard Offer

term renewable energy purchase power agreement for energy generated by solar or wind
power facilities located within the PJM Region to provide a target quantity of five percent
of the SOS load.” The RFP was issued four times before an agreement was executed and

                                  NOTICE OF COMPLAINT

                                       (November 3, 2026)

       Take notice that on November 3, 2026 pursuant to sections 206, 306, and 309 of the Federal
Power Act (“FPA”), 16 U.S.C. § 824e, 825e, and 825h, and Rule 206 of the Federal Energy
Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 CFR 385.206,
Exelon Corporation (“Exelon” or “Complainant”) filed a formal complaint against PJM
Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM” or “Respondent”) requesting that the Commission: (i) find under
FPA section 206 that the current three-year forward period of PJM’s Reliability Pricing Model
(“RPM”) is no longer just and reasonable; (ii) adopt as a replacement rate a “prompt” auction
schedule, to run two months before a given Delivery Year, starting with the 2030/2031 Delivery
Year and continuing beyond; (iii) establish a refund effective date of January 1, 2027; and (iv)
permit Fast Track processing under Rule 206(h) to facilitate a Commission order by no later than
January 31, 2027—currently the last day before the posting of the planning parameters for the
2030/31 Delivery Year Base Residual Auction.

       Exelon certifies that copies of the complaint were served on the contacts for PJM as listed
on the Commission’s list of Corporate Officials.

        Any person desiring to intervene or to protest this filing must file in accordance with Rules
211 and 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure (18 CFR 385.211, 385.214).
Protests will be considered by the Commission in determining the appropriate action to be taken,
but will not serve to make protestants parties to the proceeding. Any person wishing to become a
party must file a notice of intervention or motion to intervene, as appropriate. The Respondent’s
answer and all interventions or protests must be filed on or before the comment date. The
Respondent’s answer, motions to intervene, and protests must be served on the Complainant.

       The Commission encourages electronic submission of protests and interventions in lieu of
paper using the “eFiling” link at http://www.ferc.gov. Persons unable to file electronically should
 submit an original and 5 copies of the protest or intervention to the Federal Energy Regulatory
Commission, 888 First Street NE., Washington, DC 20426.

        This filing is accessible on-line at http://www.ferc.gov, using the “eLibrary” link and is
available for electronic review in the Commission's Public Reference Room in Washington, DC.
There is an “eSubscription” link on the Web site that enables subscribers to receive email
notification when a document is added to a subscribed docket(s). For assistance with any FERC
Online service, please email FERCOnlineSupport@ferc.gov, or call (866) 208–3676 (toll free).
For TTY, call (202) 502–8659.
